summary:
GROUNDWATCH is an interactive geospatial application exploring the hidden footprint of resource extraction in Morocco’s Haouz–High Atlas
 region. We developed a working platform that connects real NASA–ISRO NISAR radar observations, Sentinel-1 comparisons, published
 groundwater-depth records and historical mineral-site context.

 Users can explore satellite layers, switch between actual observation intervals, inspect individual measurements and trace their
 sources. The application clearly distinguishes NISAR radar phase from apparent line-of-sight displacement and explains quality controls,
 missing data and scientific limitations.

 GROUNDWATCH addresses the challenge by making complex satellite evidence accessible while separating observations from unsupported conclusions. Geographic proximity alone does not prove that pumping or mining caused surface change; the platform helps users identify questions that require further investigation and ground validation.

 This matters because surface changes can affect water resources, ecosystems and infrastructure. By making evidence and uncertainty visible together, GROUNDWATCH supports more informed environmental investigation without presenting an exploratory prototype as a validated attribution or hazard-warning system.
details:
GROUNDWATCH — The Hidden Footprint of Resource Extraction

GROUNDWATCH is a working, interactive geospatial application developed to investigate surface-change evidence in Morocco’s Haouz–High Atlas region. It brings together real NASA–ISRO NISAR radar observations, Copernicus Sentinel-1 comparisons, published groundwater-depth records, historical mineral records, earthquake information and mapped infrastructure. The live application is available at https://groundwatch-137126218728.europe-west1.run.app, and its MIT-licensed source code can be accessed at https://github.com/ItsCalin/groundwatch.

The application uses a Python processing pipeline to retrieve satellite products and metadata, verify measurement units and geographic alignment, apply quality masks, and generate compact, source-linked datasets and map images. Processing takes place outside interactive requests, allowing the website to respond quickly without requiring visitors to download large scientific products or provide Earthdata credentials. Users can explore five processed, georeferenced satellite layers, switch between actual acquisition-date pairs, inspect individual measurements alongside coordinates and quality information, examine the distributions of samples from selected intervals, and explore environmental context while reviewing sources, methods and limitations. The application contains 5,756 satellite inspection samples, including 4,522 Sentinel-1 apparent relative line-of-sight measurements in millimetres and 1,234 NISAR radar-phase samples in native radians. These quantities are kept separate rather than combined into a potentially misleading trend. A published field study also contributes 26 groundwater-depth records as additional context, although these are not presented as pumping measurements or a groundwater-decline series.

Resource extraction can be associated with environmental and infrastructure impacts, but identifying these impacts requires more than locating a mine or observing patterns on a satellite map. GROUNDWATCH addresses this challenge by providing an evidence-first workspace where users can investigate observations, understand their measurement basis and identify questions that require further research. Its intended impact is to make satellite evidence more accessible and understandable to students, researchers, communities and decision-makers while encouraging responsible scientific interpretation. The application supports investigation without claiming to establish extraction causation or provide certified hazard warnings.

The central design principle behind GROUNDWATCH is evidence before inference. Rather than inventing hotspot scores or treating all radar products as direct displacement measurements, the application makes differences between scientific observations visible and understandable. For example, the interface explains that consecutive satellite comparisons represent independent intervals rather than cumulative totals, and that the absence of statistically flagged groups does not imply an absence of measured variation. Original browse previews are kept separate from calibrated geographic overlays, and missing data are never represented as zero change. The project's innovation lies in connecting scientific traceability with accessible interaction, allowing users to move from a visible map pattern to an actual sample, its observation interval, quality information and original source.

GROUNDWATCH was developed using Python, JavaScript/JSX, HTML and CSS, with scientific processing supported by NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio/GDAL, h5py, earthaccess and fsspec. Its backend uses FastAPI and Uvicorn, while the frontend is built with React, Vite and Leaflet. The application is containerized with Docker and deployed using Google Cloud Run. Verification includes pytest, Node.js tests and Playwright/Chromium browser testing. AI coding assistants and specialist agents supported implementation, design, research, testing and documentation, but the satellite observations themselves were not AI-generated.

Throughout development, we prioritized scientific accuracy, correct measurement units, geographic alignment, data provenance, accessibility, responsive interaction, credential protection and affordable hosting. We also carefully considered the risks of overstating what the available evidence can establish. NISAR observations remain in radians because the conventions required for physical displacement conversion and correction have not yet been sufficiently validated. Sentinel-1 comparisons use independent spatial references and are therefore not presented as a cumulative time series. Groundwater records remain unmapped because their coordinate reference systems require further clarification, while historical mineral records are not treated as proof of current extraction operations. Ground validation, matched pumping or operating records, and stronger temporal analysis remain important directions for future development rather than completed results. By maintaining these scientific boundaries, GROUNDWATCH demonstrates how complex satellite observations can be transformed into an accessible, transparent and interactive investigative tool without sacrificing the accuracy and limitations of the underlying evidence.
